claim: Pests are a global threat to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and human health.
source: Pests are a global threat to biodiversity, ecosystem function, and human health.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus and cited literature in the field.

claim: Environmental and agricultural losses caused by pests have been estimated at US$120 billion annually in the US alone.
source: The environmental and agricultural losses caused by pests have been estimated at US$120 billion annually in the US alone (Pimentel et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pimentel et al., 2005.

claim: There are around 500 million human cases of mosquito-borne diseases malaria and dengue fever annually.
source: For example, there are around 500 million human cases of the mosquito-borne diseases malaria and dengue fever annually (World Health Organization, 2015; Bhatt et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2015 and Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: Conventional pest management approaches are often temporary in nature and require regular re-application.
source: The effects of these approaches are often temporary in nature and thus require regular re-application
evidence: This is a general statement about conventional pest management supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Conventional pest management approaches may have unwanted side effects on non-target species and the environment.
source: The effects of these approaches are often temporary in nature and thus require regular re-application, and may have unwanted side effects on non-target species and the environment (Bergstrom et al., 2009; Tompkins and Veltman, 2006; Innes and Barker, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergstrom et al., 2009; Tompkins and Veltman, 2006; Innes and Barker, 1999.

claim: Vertebrate culling is generally cost- and labor-intensive and can prove ineffective at low population densities.
source: Furthermore, vertebrate culling is generally cost- and labor-intensive and can prove ineffective at low population densities (Clout and Russell, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clout and Russell, 2006.

claim: Blanket pesticide application is often hampered by the evolution of resistance in target species.
source: while blanket pesticide application is often hampered by the evolution of resistance in target species (Tabashnik et al., 2008; Innes and Barker, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tabashnik et al., 2008 and Innes and Barker, 1999.

claim: The Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) is the most successful reproductive impairment technique employed to date.
source: The most successful of such techniques employed to date is the Sterile Insect Technique (SIT), whereby large quantities of sterilized males are introduced into target populations, reducing the reproductive success of the females with whom they mate (Alphey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alphey et al., 2010.

claim: A major constraint of SIT lies in the need to continuously produce and release large numbers of sterile males for sustained population suppression.
source: Although the SIT offers species-specificity, a major constraint lies in the need to continuously produce and release large numbers of sterile males for sustained population suppression, rendering eradication efforts time- and cost-intensive (Dyck et al., 2005; Alphey et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dyck et al., 2005 and Alphey et al., 2010.

claim: The goal of the TFT is to use naturally occurring mutations in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) which impair male fertility but have no effects on females to achieve multi-generational pest population suppression.
source: The goal of the TFT is to use naturally occurring mutations in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which impair male fertility but have no effects on females, to achieve multi-generational pest population suppression.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the TFT goal as described by the authors.

claim: mtDNA is typically maternally inherited.
source: Because mtDNA is typically maternally inherited (White et al., 2008; Birky, 1978)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to White et al., 2008 and Birky, 1978.

claim: Male-specific deleterious mtDNA mutations will largely escape selection in the female germ line despite their associated high fitness cost to males.
source: such male-specific deleterious mtDNA mutations will to a large degree escape selection in the female germ line despite their associated high fitness cost to males, enabling their persistent inheritance across generations (Frank and Hurst, 1996; Beekman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frank and Hurst, 1996 and Beekman et al., 2014.

claim: The TFT may offer a valuable alternative to emerging transgenic control techniques whose potential use is currently subject to debates concerning safety and regulatory concerns.
source: The TFT may thus offer a valuable alternative to emerging transgenic control techniques, whose potential use is currently subject to debates concerning safety and regulatory concerns (Oye et al., 2014; Lunshof, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oye et al., 2014 and Lunshof, 2015.

claim: The maternal inheritance of mitochondria will facilitate the accumulation of deleterious mtDNA mutations that are male-biased in their effects.
source: The conceptual framework underpinning the TFT is based on a population genetic model that shows the maternal inheritance of mitochondria will facilitate the accumulation of deleterious mtDNA mutations that are male-biased in their effects (Gemmell et al., 2004; Frank and Hurst, 1996; Beekman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gemmell et al., 2004; Frank and Hurst, 1996; and Beekman et al., 2014.

claim: The expression of fertility, longevity, and levels of nuclear gene expression are more sensitive to genetic variation in the mtDNA sequence in males than in females in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Recent empirical work in Drosophila melanogaster has substantiated this model, showing that the expression of fertility, longevity, and levels of nuclear gene expression are more sensitive to genetic variation in the mtDNA sequence in males than in females (Camus et al., 2012; Yee et al., 2013; Innocenti et al., 2011; Camus et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Camus et al., 2012; Yee et al., 2013; Innocenti et al., 2011; and Camus et al., 2015.

claim: Particular mtDNA haplotypes have been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males but with no apparent effects on female fertility in Drosophila.
source: Furthermore, particular mtDNA haplotypes have now been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males, but with no apparent effects on female fertility, in Drosophila (Dowling et al., 2015; Yee et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2016; Wolff et al., 2016b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dowling et al., 2015; Yee et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2016; and Wolff et al., 2016b.

claim: Particular mtDNA haplotypes have been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males but with no apparent effects on female fertility in seed beetles.
source: Furthermore, particular mtDNA haplotypes have now been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males, but with no apparent effects on female fertility, in Drosophila (Dowling et al., 2015; Yee et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2016; Wolff et al., 2016b), seed beetles (Dowling et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dowling et al., 2007.

claim: Particular mtDNA haplotypes have been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males but with no apparent effects on female fertility in hares.
source: Furthermore, particular mtDNA haplotypes have now been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males, but with no apparent effects on female fertility, in Drosophila (Dowling et al., 2015; Yee et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2016; Wolff et al., 2016b), seed beetles (Dowling et al., 2007), hares (Smith et al., 2010)

claim: Particular mtDNA haplotypes have been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males but with no apparent effects on female fertility in humans.
source: Furthermore, particular mtDNA haplotypes have now been associated with sub- or complete-infertility in males, but with no apparent effects on female fertility, in Drosophila (Dowling et al., 2015; Yee et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2016; Wolff et al., 2016b), seed beetles (Dowling et al., 2007), hares (Smith et al., 2010), and humans (Ruiz-Pesini et al., 2000).

claim: TFT haplotypes are predicted to cause suppression across a wide range of life-histories.

claim: The Brownsville mitochondrial haplotype has been associated with perturbed spermatogenesis and sperm maturation.
source: Building on those initial models (Gemmell et al., 2013), empirical attention has focused on a particular mitochondrial haplotype sourced from a population of D. melanogaster in Brownsville (USA), which has been associated with perturbed spermatogenesis and sperm maturation (Clancy et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clancy et al., 2011.

claim: The Brownsville haplotype confers complete male sterility when placed alongside one isogenic nuclear background.
source: and is known to confer complete male sterility when placed alongside one isogenic nuclear background (i.e. a nuclear background devoid of any allelic variation; Clancy et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clancy et al., 2011.

source: The SNP located in the mt:Cyt-b gene is non-synonymous, causing an amino acid change (Ala278→Thr) in complex III of the mitochondrial electron transfer chain
